at elske.explanation: "At elske" means to love, and it is a strong word that Danes mostly keep for people they truly care about: "Jeg elsker dig" (I love you). For things and activities, Danes usually say "Jeg kan godt lide" (I like) or "Jeg holder af". Using "elske" for pizza is possible, but it is more playful.

sentence.en: I love you.

forms.da: Jeg har et brev i e-Boks.
forms.en: I have a letter in e-Boks.

e-boks.explanation: e-Boks is the digital mailbox where public offices, banks and many companies send official letters in Denmark. It is an en-word, so you say "e-Boksen" for "the e-Boks". Most people check it often, because important letters from the tax office or doctor arrive there.

sentence.da: Jeg har fået et brev i **e-Boks**.
sentence.en: I have received a letter in e-Boks.

efter.explanation: "Efter" means after, for time and for order. It also appears in many verb phrases where English uses "for": "lede efter" (look for), "spørge efter" (ask for) and "længes efter" (long for). When a whole sentence with its own verb follows, you need "efter at", as in "efter at jeg kom hjem".

sentence.en: We go for a walk after dinner.

egen.explanation: "Egen" means own, and it goes with words like "min" (my) or "din" (your). It changes to match: "egen" for en-words, "eget" for et-words, and "egne" for more than one. For example, "mit eget værelse" is "my own room". It is also used to stress something is yours alone.

sentence.en: I want my own room.

ekstra.explanation: "Ekstra" means extra, and it never changes its form, whether the word after it is an en-word or an et-word. It can describe a thing ("en ekstra stol") or add to another word ("ekstra god"). Handy in shops and restaurants.

sentence.en: Can I have an extra chair?

eller.explanation: "Eller" means or, and it joins two choices. At the end of a question, "eller?" asks for agreement, a bit like "right?" in English. Do not mix it up with "ellers", which means "otherwise". It is also used in "enten ... eller" (either ... or).

sentence.en: Do you want tea or coffee?

forms.da: skynd dig, ellers kommer vi for sent
forms.en: hurry up, or else we will be late

ellers.explanation: "Ellers" means otherwise or or else. It is used to say what happens if something does not happen, or to mean "apart from that". Do not mix it up with "eller", which only means "or" and joins two choices.

sentence.da: Tag en jakke på, **ellers** bliver du kold.
sentence.en: Put on a jacket, or else you will get cold.

elleve.explanation: Means "eleven". It is the first of the numbers that does not follow a pattern. Say it with a soft "v" in the middle. The next, "tolv", is also unique. After that, the teens end in "-ten", like "tretten".

sentence.en: It's eleven o'clock.

en e-mail.explanation: "En e-mail" is an email and is written with a hyphen. You say "en e-mail" and "e-mailen". In daily speech people often shorten it to "en mail". You "sender" (send) and "modtager" (receive) emails.

sentence.en: I have sent you an email.

en eftermiddag.explanation: "En eftermiddag" is an afternoon, the part of the day from lunch until evening. "Om eftermiddagen" means in the afternoon as a habit, and "i eftermiddag" means this afternoon. The word is built from "efter" (after) and "middag" (midday).

sentence.en: We drink coffee in the afternoon.

en elefant.explanation: "En elefant" is an elephant. It is spelled with an "f" and sounds quite like the English word. Note that Danish has no "an", only "en" for en-words. You can see elephants at the zoo or on a safari.

sentence.en: The elephant is a very big animal.

en elev.explanation: "En elev" is a pupil, a child or young person who goes to school. It can also mean a trainee or apprentice at a workplace. Adults who study at university are usually called "en studerende" or "en student" rather than "elev".

sentence.en: There are twenty pupils in the class.

en elevator.explanation: "Elevator" is a lift in a building. Danes often say "en elevator" but also "en lift", and both are fine and understood everywhere. You go "med elevatoren" (by the elevator) up or down a floor. The stairs are "trappen".

sentence.en: We take the elevator up.

en enkeltbillet.explanation: "Enkeltbillet" is a one-way ticket, for a trip in only one direction. "Enkelt" means single, so it is a single ticket. The opposite is "en returbillet" (return ticket). In a train or bus you say "En enkeltbillet, tak."

sentence.en: A one-way ticket to Copenhagen, please.

en euro.explanation: "En euro" is a euro, the money used in many European countries. In Danish it usually stays the same after a number: "ti euro". Denmark does not use the euro. Danes pay with "kroner".

sentence.en: It costs twenty euros.

end.explanation: "End" means "than" and is used when you compare two things, as in "Hun er højere end mig" (She is taller than me). It comes after a describing word with an "-ere" ending, like "større" (bigger) or "bedre" (better). Watch out: "end" (than) is spelled with a d and sounds close to "en" (a). Don't use "som" for "than".

sentence.en: He is older than me.

endnu.explanation: "Endnu" means yet or still. "Ikke endnu" is not yet: "Jeg er ikke færdig endnu" (I am not finished yet). It can also mean even more, as in "endnu bedre" (even better), and "endnu en gang" means one more time. A close word is "stadig", which usually means still.

sentence.en: I am not finished yet.

eneste.explanation: "Eneste" means only or single, as in "the only one". It is almost always used with "den", "det" or "de" (the): "den eneste" is the only one for en-words, "det eneste" for et-words. It has no separate form for "a", so it is not used with "en" or "et". Not the same as "kun", which means just or only as a small word.

sentence.da: Det er den **eneste** bus i dag.
sentence.en: It is the only bus today.

forms.en: Come and visit me some day!

engang.explanation: "Engang" means "once" or "some day", for a time that is not clear. "Der var engang" is how fairy tales begin (Once upon a time). "Kom og besøg os engang" is a friendly "Come and visit sometime". Do not mix it up with "en gang" (two words), which means "one time".

sentence.en: I once lived in Italy.

engelsk.explanation: "Engelsk" means English. It is the word for the language and for things from England. As a school lesson, you say "Jeg har engelsk". Like all languages in Danish, it is written with a small letter. Say "Taler du engelsk?" to ask "Do you speak English?".

sentence.en: Do you speak English?

england.explanation: "England" is England. Place names like this are written with a capital letter and used without "the": "i England" means "in England" and "til England" means "to England". A person is "en englænder" and the language is "engelsk". Do not use it for the whole of the UK; that is "Storbritannien".

sentence.en: I have lived in England.

enogtyve.explanation: "Enogtyve" is twenty-one. Danish says the small number first: "en og tyve" means one and twenty, written as one word. The same pattern is used for 22 to 29 and in the 30s to 90s. For larger numbers it is the same idea: "toogtyve" (22).

sentence.en: My son is twenty-one years old.

forms.da: Enten i dag eller i morgen.
Enten er du med, eller også er du ikke.
forms.en: Either you are in, or you are not.

enten…eller.explanation: "Enten … eller" means "either … or" and offers two choices. You put "enten" before the first choice and "eller" before the second. When the choice is between two whole sentences, it is common to say "eller også" for the second part. A tip: "både … og" (both … and) is the opposite idea, because there you take both options.

sentence.en: We can either walk or take the bus.

er det ...?.explanation: A simple question pattern: put "er" first to ask "is it...?". There is no extra word like "do" in Danish, you just swap the order. Fill the gap with whatever you want to ask about. Start with "er det" and add a word, such as "er det rigtigt?" (is that right?).

sentence.en: Is it far from here?

er du sikker?.explanation: "Er du sikker?" means "are you sure?" and is a handy question when you doubt something or want to check. The word "sikker" means "sure" or "safe". Answer "ja, helt sikker" or "nej, jeg er ikke sikker". Use "er I sikre?" for several people.

sentence.da: **Er du sikker?** Det er en lang tur.
sentence.en: Are you sure? It is a long trip.

et efternavn.explanation: "Et efternavn" is your last name, the family name that comes after the first name. "Efter" means "after". Many Danish surnames end in "-sen", such as Hansen or Jensen. On forms you will see "Efternavn".

sentence.en: What is your last name?

et efterår.explanation: Et efterår is autumn (or fall in American English), the season after summer. In Danish, "the autumn" is "efteråret". It is built from "efter" (after) and "år" (year), so it is the part of the year that comes after summer. Use "om efteråret" for "in the autumn" in general. It is often rainy and windy in Denmark then.

sentence.en: The leaves fall in the autumn.

et enkeltværelse.explanation: An "enkeltværelse" is a hotel room for one person. The word is built from "enkelt" (single) and "værelse" (room). You will use it when booking a hotel or hostel. The pair to it is "et dobbeltværelse", a room for two.

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne booke et **enkeltværelse** til to nætter.
sentence.en: I would like to book a single room for two nights.

europa.explanation: "Europa" is Europe. Like other place names, it is written with a capital letter and used without "the". You say "i Europa" (in Europe), "til Europa" (to Europe). The people are "europæere" and the describing word is "europæisk". Denmark is a part of Europe and of the EU.

sentence.en: Denmark is in Europe.

europæisk.explanation: "Europæisk" is written with a small letter, and the plural is "europæiske". A European person is "en europæer". In the news you will often meet it in "den Europæiske Union" (the European Union), where it is capitalised because it is part of a name.

sentence.en: Denmark is a European country.
